transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-11-20 15:00 PST / Duration: 72 mins
Attendees: Jordan Blake, Priya Menon, Liam Ortiz (Redwood) — Maya Chen, Ethan Ross, Sofia Alvarez (Arcturus)
Notes: call recorded, auto-transcript (medium quality).

00:00 Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, i think we have about 70 minutes, um goal today is to walk through p95/p99 tail causes you're seeing and map a plan for a pilot
00:18 Maya: thanks, yeah we've been seeing spikes at p99 that are well outside our expectations, sometimes double the p95, esp under heavy concurrency
00:30 Priya: can you give us the quick topology? like clients -> LB -> inference -> maybe cache layer?
00:40 Ethan: sure, we have a public API fronted by an NLB, then a fleet of gRPC workers in a private subnet, then calls to a Redis cluster for prefix caching and an internal KV service, cross-AZ for redundancy so sometimes there are extra hops
00:58 Liam: ok so cross-AZ + external NAT and encryption could add tail variance, also if Redis misses you get the full model path which is heavier
01:12 Sofia: our typical request is 1.2k tokens max, avg 280, and we do streaming on the UI for user-facing chat, but internal batch jobs use non-streaming. tail happens in both paths
01:28 Priya: streaming adds complexity because you have incremental token generation RPCs and flushing; non-streaming is single request/response so different network profiles — do you have instrumentation that separates streaming chunk latency vs model generation time?
01:45 Ethan: we emit traces but they sometimes collapse at the LB, we can add finer sampling. we do see spikes when Redis gets evicted or when the KV cache miss rate jumps during cold-starts after deploys
02:02 Jordan: sounds like three big buckets: network hops/cross-AZ, cache miss cold paths, and GPU-side stalls (kernel selection, quantized kernel fallbacks). can we walk through each?
02:15 Priya: yeah network first — cross-AZ means extra millisecond-range hops. if your NLB does health/flow handling that can add variance, also mTLS/TLS handshakes if not re-used cause tail outliers
02:30 Maya: we use mTLS with short-lived certs rotated, client connections are re-used mostly but some requests spawn new connections from lambda-like frontends
02:45 Liam: that explains spikes — connection cold starts + TLS handshake + additional RTTs. recommendation: keep long-lived connections, enable tcp keepalive and tls session resumption. also consider co-locating the Redis cluster in same AZ or using local hot-keys for the most frequent prefixes.
03:05 Priya: on KV cache behavior — prefix hits are super cheap: local memhit -> small lookup -> return. but when you miss, you need to populate KV from model output or fallback to full inference path which includes attention cache allocation and kv cache warmup; that can be 50–200ms extra depending on model size
03:25 Sofia: our miss rate went from 4% to 18% during bursts — could autoscaling cause eviction?
03:32 Ethan: yes we scale Redis up and down with memory-based policies; during scaling windows we see higher evictions
03:40 Priya: for that you want a sticky cache topology or better, an LRU with proactive pre-warming for hot prefixes, and also use async population so you don't block the user flow. we can show a microbench comparing blocking vs async population.
03:56 Jordan: quantization — have you tried int8/4bit? you mentioned memory pressure earlier
04:04 Sofia: we tried 4-bit quant on a staging model, throughput increased but tail got worse occasionally — some rare requests blew up with a 300ms penalty
04:14 Priya: that tracks — quantized kernels sometimes use fallback paths for certain ops (sparse attention patterns, rotary embeddings) and the fallback code may not be vectorized. Also quantization can change memory access patterns that stress the allocator. we recommend model-specific kernel tuning and profiling; Redwood picks kernels based on sequence length distribution to avoid those fallbacks when possible.
04:40 Liam: another trick is mixed-precision: keep keys/values in fp16 while storing activations quantized, that reduces worst-case fallback triggers. but it requires validation for quality/regression.
05:00 Ethan: what about batching? we thought larger batches always reduce cost but tail sometimes spikes when small requests wait for batch windows
05:10 Priya: yes batching is a trade-off: larger batch windows reduce token latency for high-throughput steady state but add queueing latency for low-latency requests. Redwood supports dynamic scheduling: small tail-sensitive queues served on low-latency nodes, and larger batch pools for throughput. you can route requests by latency SLO tags.
05:32 Maya: streaming vs non-streaming — does streaming hurt p99 because of incremental flushes?
05:40 Priya: it can, because streaming opens sustained per-token RPCs and each chunk has overhead. However you can mitigate by local chunk buffering and server-side streaming where we aggregate small generations before flush if latency budget allows. also progressive KV caching helps: if prefix hits you return immediately then stream next tokens quickly.
06:05 Sofia: we saw p99 jumps when a single request expected many tokens and we also had a bad prefix miss; the pipeline compounded — network + cache miss + long decode = disastrous tail
06:18 Liam: isolating long-tail requests to dedicated GPU pools helps — you don't let them pollute latency-sensitive pools. Redwood Dedicated can reserve nodes for low-latency traffic and separate heavy batch jobs.
06:32 Jordan: question on measurements — do you measure p95/p99 on the client side or at the server? they can differ because of network hops
06:40 Ethan: currently server-side metrics, but we can add client-side synthetic load to measure end-to-end; that would capture TLS and NLB hops
06:48 Priya: we recommend both. server-side helps diagnose model/runtime; client-side gives you true user experience. also histogram tail analysis and trace sampling is key — we usually capture additional spans for TLS handshake, connection open, redis lookup, model forward, and streaming flush.
07:10 Maya: one practical ask — can you run a microbench for us that simulates our token distribution, with and without prefix hits, streaming vs aggregate, across int8 vs fp16?
07:22 Priya: yes we can; we'll run the KV-cache microbench and a streaming microbench. we'll provide CSVs and a comparison sheet.
07:30 Liam: we should also check kernel selection thresholds: if your typical sequence length is ~1.2k tokens we might choose kernels optimized for longer context which change memory layout; we'll include that in the report.
07:45 Ethan: are there any Redwood-specific knobs for network that help? like tls offload or lane pinning?
07:52 Jordan: for private deployments you can colocate the Redis and inference in the same subnet and use ENI-local routing, reduce NAT, and enable mTLS session resumption. for hosted we offer regional routing and dedicated capacity to reduce cross-AZ traffic.
08:12 Sofia: for on-prem/workload isolation, what about HSM/KMS integration — does that add latency?
08:18 Priya: KMS calls for key retrieval are small but if done per-request they can add tens of ms; we recommend caching keys in memory with TTL and using an HSM for periodic rewraps. we'll include recommended KMS patterns in the security doc.
08:35 Maya: about rollout — we need validations for quality regression when toggling quantization or new kernel picks
08:42 Liam: Redwood Optimize can do A/B rollouts with eval harnesses and prompt sets; you can register fail-on-regression rules to prevent rollout. we also record per-prompt quality metrics.
08:58 Jordan: ok to recap — Priya runs KV and streaming microbenches, we share the benchmark spreadsheet and kernel picks, Arcturus shares topology and traces. Redwood sends security whitepaper and pricing. pilot kickoff next week if numbers look good.
09:18 Ethan: one last Q, anything around pre-warm vs cold-starts for GPUs? we've seen 1–2s cold spikes after idle windows
09:28 Priya: cold starts are expensive; keep a minimal warm pool or use tiny keep-alive load to keep WGpu contexts hot. also use quick-start checkpoints to reduce model load times; we can show numbers for warm vs cold.
09:45 Maya: great thanks everyone, looking forward to the microbench results and the follow-up
09:52 Jordan: thanks all, we'll follow up with artifacts and set the pilot date
09:58 (call ends)
